gallery.filename: Bengasi court square 0824b.jpg
gallery.title: File:Bengasi court square 0824b.jpg
gallery.description: Crowd at the Court house square in Benghazi, April 2011. The square was a place for gathering, demonstrations and organisation of the uprise movement. The walls of the court house are draped with pictures of casualties of the fighting, as well as former executions by Gaddafi, mourners passing by. Flags and souvenirs are sold at a table in the center. The red-white flag on the left marks the al-Ahly soccer club that was destroyed by Gaddafi's order in 2000, and three leaders executed, after insubordination.

gallery.filename: "Martyr's Tie" - Flickr - Al Jazeera English.jpg
gallery.title: File:"Martyr's Tie" - Flickr - Al Jazeera English.jpg
gallery.description:
Mohammed Tajouri became well-known around Ajdabiya after arriving from Benghazi and staying through the fighting. He took a gun and fought at the front lines during the see-saw battles for control of the town. At one point, residents said, he looped and knotted a blue rope around his thigh and calf, making a "Martyr's Tie" around his right leg that was meant to prevent him running away from the front line should he become scared.

He too came to the makeshift salon at Ajdabiya's western gate for a buzz.

gallery.description: Amir Khaled, 18, stopped by the makeshift barber shop at Ajdabiya's western gate to get a buzz. He said he wants Muammar Gaddafi to be gone by the time his hair grows back.

gallery.description: The modified pick-up truck, or "technical," is a trademark of modern, unconventional warfare. Both rebels and government forces have used them extensively during the conflict. This one is carrying an anti-aircraft gun, ammunition, and petrol stored in plastic barrels.

gallery.filename: Brega checkpoint - Flickr - Al Jazeera English.jpg
gallery.title: File:Brega checkpoint - Flickr - Al Jazeera English.jpg
gallery.description: At the main checkpoint near the strategic oil town of Brega, men with what appeared to be better equipment and gear than their untrained comrades began to assemble. They wore emblems indicating their position as engineers or paratroopers and said they were defected "special forces" from Benghazi who were awaiting orders. Despite their more impressive appearance, they still seemed to lack the kind of discipline one might see in Western militaries, or perhaps even Gaddafi's own forces.

gallery.description: Many rebels have told reporters that they never fired, much less held, a gun before the Libyan uprising broke out on February 17. Now they are on the front lines of the revolt, handling heavy weaponry acquired from army stockpiles.

gallery.filename: Brega hospital - Flickr - Al Jazeera English.jpg
gallery.title: File:Brega hospital - Flickr - Al Jazeera English.jpg
gallery.description: A man alleged by hospital staff to be a pro-Gaddafi fighter lies dead on the floor of a one-room morgue. Though he wore green, army-style trousers, the rest of his clothes appeared to bear no hint of a standard uniform.

gallery.filename: Brega hospital - Flickr - Al Jazeera English (1).jpg
gallery.title: File:Brega hospital - Flickr - Al Jazeera English (1).jpg
gallery.description: Hussein Omran, a 14-year-old shepherd, was also injured by shrapnel during the early-morning attack on Brega by pro-Gaddafi forces. His 12-year-old brother Hassan was reportedly among those who died. Here, as journalists swarmed into the room where Omran and his 7-year-old brother were being triaged, nurses coaxed him into showing the V-for-victory sign.
